questions.title: Autoscale a model service on queue and cache signals
questions.prompt: Your model service runs as a plain Deployment with an autoscaler on CPU use. During a traffic spike the autoscaler added replicas late, kept adding them while the new pods were still loading weights, and a liveness probe restarted the busiest pod in the middle of the spike. Redesign the scaling and the probes.
questions.short: Scale on the engine's own signals, not on CPU: the count of waiting requests and the KV cache usage say that a server is saturated long before CPU does. Give the startup probe a window longer than your measured cold start, so that a loading pod is neither sent traffic nor restarted, and make the liveness probe cheap, so that a busy server does not lose its busiest pod to a probe that waited in the queue. Keep the weights and the compile cache on persistent storage, so that a new replica is ready in a fraction of the time.
questions.full:
### Why CPU is the wrong signal

GPU load is not CPU load. A saturated engine shows waiting requests above zero and cache usage near one while the CPU looks calm. The vLLM manual says this directly about the plain Deployment: it routes at random and scales on the wrong signal. The routing layers that the manual lists read `vllm:num_requests_waiting`, `vllm:num_requests_running` and `vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc` to pick a replica, and an autoscaler should read the same series.

### Read the signals in pairs

| Reading | Meaning |
|---|---|
| waiting above 0, cache usage below 0.9 | the batch size or the token budget limits admission, not memory |
| waiting above 0, cache usage near 1 | the pool limits admission, so add memory or replicas |
| slow first token with nothing waiting | long prompts or a slow tokenizer, not a capacity problem |
| preemptions with long answers | running requests grow until the pool runs out |

The second row is a reason to add a replica, because the pool is full. On the first row, raise the batch limit or the token budget first, while the pool has room. If the queue stays after that, or the limit is already where the latency target needs it, add a replica, because each replica brings its own batch limit and token budget.

### Probes that match a slow start

The manual's example gives the startup probe 90 checks at 10 second intervals, which is 15 minutes, and notes that its own machine took about 8 minutes for a first start. Set the window from your measured cold start. For readiness, send one short real request, which proves the engine can generate, or use the ready endpoint on an engine that has one. For liveness, use a cheap health path. The SGLang manual turns generation off in the health endpoint, because a probe that generates waits in the queue under load, times out after 20 seconds, and marks a busy server unhealthy. In one incident each failed probe also left an orphan request in the scheduler, so the probes added to the load they were meant to detect.

### Stop the overshoot

New pods take minutes to load. The autoscaler sees the signal still high and adds more. Give it a stabilization window at least as long as the cold start, cap the replicas added per step, and shorten the cold start itself: weights on local disk, the compile cache on a persistent volume, and a preload before the server takes traffic. The cold start lesson adds the warm pool for the interactive path, so that the first replica is never a cold one.

### Scale down without losing work

Remove the pod from the load balancer, send SIGTERM to the main process only, and set a grace period at least as long as the longest request at the output cap. A forced kill, or a signal to the whole process group, drops every running request.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Which pair of readings says the pool is the bottleneck, not the batch limit? Expected: waiting requests above zero with cache usage near one. With cache usage below 0.9, the batch size or the token budget limits admission instead.
- **Level 3:** Why does a generating health probe hurt under load? Expected: its request waits in the queue like any other, times out, and marks a busy server unhealthy. In one incident each failed probe also left an orphan request behind.
- **Level 4:** How do you keep the autoscaler from overshooting during a cold start? Expected: a stabilization window at least as long as the measured cold start, a cap on replicas added per step, and a shorter cold start from persistent weights and compile caches.
- **Level 4:** What does a scale-down need so that no request is lost? Expected: remove the pod from the load balancer, send SIGTERM to the main process only, and a grace period at least as long as the longest request at the output cap.
questions.wrong:
- "Scale on GPU utilization instead of CPU." Utilization can read high while requests wait and low while the pool is full. The queue and the cache usage are the signals the engine exposes for this.
- "Make the liveness probe stricter so that bad pods restart faster." Under load a strict probe restarts healthy, busy pods. The fix is a cheap probe and a long startup window.
- "Add replicas faster to beat the spike." Replicas that take minutes to load add nothing during the spike and cost money after it. Shorten the cold start and keep a warm margin.

questions.title: Sort a workload into interactive, async or batch
questions.prompt: A team runs its nightly report pipeline through the same synchronous endpoint as the chat product, because the pipeline is production. How do you classify model workloads, and where does this one belong?
questions.short: Sort every workload by the latency its user accepts, not by where it runs. Interactive work has a user waiting for the first token and stays synchronous with prompt caching, and semi-interactive work returns in minutes through an async queue. Anything whose user can wait for the full promise belongs on the batch API, which gives a 50 percent discount with a return promised within 24 hours and typical in a few hours. The nightly report is batch when a return at the 24-hour limit still meets its deadline, or when a synchronous fallback covers a late batch.
questions.full:
### The three lanes

| Lane | The user | The path |
|---|---|---|
| interactive | waits for the first token | synchronous, with prompt caching |
| semi-interactive | submits and checks back in minutes | async queue, with a synchronous fallback |
| batch | expects the result by morning or end of day | batch API, with cached input stacked on top |

### The misclassification

The lesson's rule is blunt: production is not a latency spec, the SLA is. The common mistake is to call everything interactive because it runs in production. Its cousin is the partial-interactivity trap: a report with a refresh button that users happily wait ten minutes for, shipped as a synchronous call. The lesson puts 50 concurrent refreshes at 10x the cost of the same report batched and delivered by mail.

### What batch promises

A return within 24 hours, with a typical return of a few hours, because the provider runs the batch when its capacity is idle. The lesson calls this asynchronous, not slow.

### Stack it with caching

A nightly pipeline shares one system prompt across every call. Cache that prefix, run the pipeline on batch, and the lesson's arithmetic lands near 10 percent of the synchronous uncached cost. Its opening example takes a nightly pipeline from a four-hour synchronous run to a batch run at about 9 percent of the bill with three configuration changes.

### The other trap

Batch file formats differ per provider, so one batch client needs an adapter per provider, and a gateway that advertises multi-provider batch still wraps the raw formats.
questions.followups:
- **Level 1:** Which question sorts a workload into a lane? Expected: what a wait of a day means to this user. If they would not notice, it is batch.
- **Level 2:** A user clicks refresh on a health report and waits ten minutes without complaint. Which lane? Expected: semi-interactive at most, and batch if the report can arrive by mail. Shipping it synchronous is the partial-interactivity trap.
- **Level 2:** Why does the lesson call batch asynchronous rather than slow? Expected: the promise is a return within a day, and the typical return is a few hours, because the provider runs it when capacity is idle.
- **Level 3:** What breaks when you write one batch client for two providers? Expected: the file formats differ, so you need an adapter per provider.
questions.wrong:
- "It runs in production, so it is interactive." Production is where it runs. The lane comes from the latency the user accepts.
- "Batch means the answer takes a day." The promise is within a day. The typical return is a few hours.
- "A 50 percent discount is not worth the complexity." On a shared prefix it stacks with caching to about a tenth of the synchronous cost, which the lesson calls the cheapest lever that nobody pulls.

questions.title: Controls that stop a bug from spending the month
questions.prompt: Last month a bug in a retry loop spent the whole monthly model budget in two days, and nobody saw it until the invoice. Design the controls that stop the next one, with the thresholds and what each threshold does.
questions.short: Put a cost tracker on every call and a ladder of thresholds on top of it. At 70 percent of the budget alert, at 85 percent throttle so that every request goes to the cheapest model, and at 95 percent stop so that only cached answers are served and new calls are refused. In front of the ladder, add a rate limit and a daily spend cap per tenant, and a kill switch that pauses a tenant whose spend jumps far above its own history.
questions.full:
### The tracker

Every call logs the timestamp, the model, the input and output tokens, the latency, the computed cost, the user, the cache status and the request category. The running total against the monthly budget is the input of every control below. A check that runs nightly is too slow, because a retry loop spends a day's budget in minutes.

### The budget ladder

| Share spent | Action |
|---|---|
| 70 percent | send an alert |
| 85 percent | throttle: route every request to the cheapest model |
| 95 percent | stop: serve cached responses only, refuse new requests |

Each step buys time for the next. The alert gives people a chance to act, the throttle keeps the service up at lower quality while the spend slows, and the stop protects the budget when nobody acted.

### The per-tenant ladder

The FinOps lesson gives three controls per tenant for a multi-tenant product:

1. A rate limit at 2 to 3 times the expected peak, with a rate-limit status and a retry header. The tenant feels friction and gets no surprise bill.
2. A daily spend cap at 1.5 to 3 times the contracted ceiling. Crossing it tightens the rate limit and alerts customer success.
3. A kill switch when the spend z-score against the tenant's own baseline passes 4. It pauses the tenant and pages on-call.

The z-score matters because tenants differ by orders of magnitude. A fixed amount is noise for a large tenant and a month of budget for a small one.

### Test the ladder

The caching lesson's exercise simulates 1,000 requests against a budget of 1.00 dollars and checks that each threshold fires. Its projection exercise forecasts the month from the trailing 7-day average and alerts when the forecast exceeds the budget by more than 20 percent. Both belong in the test suite, because a circuit breaker that was never tripped on purpose is a hope.

### Where it runs

At the gateway, where every call passes. A control that lives in one application misses the application that has the bug.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why three thresholds and not one hard stop? Expected: the alert gives people time, the throttle buys more time at lower quality, and the stop protects the budget. One hard stop surprises users with no warning.
- **Level 3:** What changes for users during the throttle step? Expected: quality, because every request goes to the cheapest model. The service stays up while the spend slows.
- **Level 3:** Why is the kill switch relative to the tenant's history? Expected: tenants differ by orders of magnitude. A z-score catches a jump for a small tenant and ignores a normal day for a large one.
- **Level 4:** The retry bug spent the budget in two days. Which control fires first? Expected: the daily spend cap or the z-score kill switch fires on the first day. The monthly ladder would only have warned at 70 percent.
questions.wrong:
- "Set a hard limit at the provider and stop there." The provider limit stops every tenant at once with no warning. The ladder degrades first and isolates the tenant.
- "An alert to the team channel is enough." The incident is a bug at night. The throttle and the stop act without a person.
- "Check the budget nightly." A retry loop spends a day's budget in minutes. The tracker has to run on every call.

questions.title: How many reads a cached prefix needs to pay off
questions.prompt: Your provider charges a 25 percent premium to write a prefix into its cache, and it bills a cache read at a tenth of the normal input price. The cache lives for five minutes. A one-hour variant costs twice the normal input price to write. How many reads does each variant need to pay off, and what rule do you give the team?
questions.short: With the five-minute cache, one write and one read average 0.675 of the normal cost per request, a saving of about 32 percent, so the cache pays off on the first read. One write and ten reads average 0.205, about 80 percent saved. The one-hour cache charges 2x for the write, so that block needs two reads before it comes out ahead. The rule: cache anything you expect to reuse at least three times inside its lifetime.
questions.full:
### The arithmetic

A write costs 1.25 times the normal input price, and a read costs 0.1 times it.

- One write and one read: the two requests average 0.675 of the normal price. That is 32 percent saved on the first read already.
- One write and ten reads: the requests average 0.205 of the normal price, about 80 percent saved.
- The one-hour cache writes at 2 times the normal price. With one read the average sits above the normal price, and with two reads it falls below. The lesson says the one-hour block pays back fast on any batch that reuses the prefix more than five times.

Three reuses inside the lifetime clear the break-even on either variant, which is the rule the lesson gives.

### What breaks the arithmetic

- A prefix that differs by one token on every request, because of a timestamp, a request id or a reshuffled tool list. Every request writes and none reads.
- A block below the minimum cacheable size, which is 1,024 tokens on the provider in the lesson. A smaller block silently does not cache.
- Requests that arrive in parallel before the first write has landed. Each one pays the write premium, and none reads.

### Verify it

Read the usage fields on every response: the tokens written to the cache and the tokens read from it. In CI, assert that the second identical request reads more than zero. On the dashboard, split input tokens into cached and uncached, or a traffic drop will look like a cache win.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why does the five-minute cache pay off on the first read? Expected: the write premium is a quarter and the read saves nine tenths, so the two together already average below the normal price.
- **Level 2:** When does the one-hour cache make sense? Expected: a batch job that reuses the prefix across runs more than five minutes apart, more than five times.
- **Level 3:** Input tokens are down and the bill is flat. What is wrong with the dashboard? Expected: it does not split cached from uncached input, so a drop in traffic looks like a cache win.
- **Level 3:** Ten parallel requests share a prefix that nobody has cached yet. What happens to the arithmetic? Expected: all ten pay the write premium and none reads, so the cache costs more than no cache. Send one request first, then the rest.
questions.wrong:
- "Caching always saves money." A prefix written once and never read costs 25 percent more than no cache.
- "Pick the one-hour cache, it lasts longer." It writes at twice the normal input price, so a block read once costs more than without the cache.
- "Mark the whole prompt as cacheable." The user message changes every time, so the match ends at the first differing token, and a block below the minimum size does not cache at all.

questions.title: The router saved half the bill, then the escalations climbed
questions.prompt: Six months ago a cascading router cut the bill by more than half with no measurable quality loss. Since then the escalation rate has crept from 8 percent to 22 percent, and a sales engineer reports that a competitor's demo now answers better than your product. Diagnose it.
questions.short: The traffic drifted and the router did not. Its classifier learned the question mix of six months ago, users now ask longer and harder questions, and the cheap model's first pass fails its own confidence check more often, which is what the rising escalation rate records. Quality fell silently on the requests that were not escalated. Gate every route with online quality metrics, retrain the classifier on current traffic, and treat an escalation rate above about 30 percent as proof that the cheap model is over-routed.
questions.full:
### The failure mode the lesson warns about

A route sends a large share of traffic to a weaker model. Over months the task distribution shifts: users get more sophisticated and ask longer questions. The router does not notice, because its classifier was trained on the earlier quarter. Quality drops by a few percent on reasoning tasks, nobody complains loudly enough, and the team finds out from a competitor benchmark. The lesson's numbers for the pattern: 40 percent routed cheap, a 3 to 5 percent quality drop, unnoticed for a quarter.

### Three causes of a rising escalation rate

1. **Distribution shift.** More long prompts and more multi-step questions. The lesson's length signal says prompts above 4K tokens often need the frontier model, and prompts under 500 tokens usually do not. If the mix moved up, more first passes fail.
2. **The cheap model changed.** A provider update behind the same alias, or a routine version bump, moves the confidence signal and the refusal behavior.
3. **Stale thresholds.** The confidence cutoff and the embedding set of known-hard questions were tuned on old traffic.

Each cause has its own fix: retrain the classifier on recent labeled traffic, pin the model version and log the served model on every call, and refresh the hard set and the cutoff on a new eval.

### Gates on live traffic

The lesson gates routes with live signals, not with the offline set:

- thumbs up and down per route;
- an automated judge on a 5 percent held-out sample per route;
- the escalation rate, where a cascade that kicks up more than 30 percent of requests is over-routing;
- the refusal rate per route.

### What the cascade now costs

The cascade pattern was designed for about 1.2 times the median latency and about 2 times on the escalated share, with roughly 10 percent escalated. At 22 percent escalated, a fifth of the requests pay for two model calls and the slow path, so the saving shrank while the quality fell.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why did the offline eval not catch the loss? Expected: the eval set was built from the old distribution. It scores the model on questions that users no longer ask.
- **Level 3:** Which online metric gives the earliest warning? Expected: the escalation rate per route. It rises as the cheap model fails its own confidence check more often, before the thumbs or a judge sample show the loss.
- **Level 4:** The provider updated the cheap model behind the same alias. How do you know? Expected: a step change in escalations or judge scores on a date with no deploy on your side. Pin the model version and log the served model on every call.
- **Level 4:** Where do you set the alarm on the escalation rate? Expected: near the design target, about 10 percent escalated for the cascade pattern, with the lesson's 30 percent as the hard line for over-routing.
questions.wrong:
- "The cheap model got worse, swap it." Possible, and the first suspect is the router's stale classifier against drifted traffic.
- "Quality is fine, the eval score did not move." The eval set comes from the old distribution and cannot see the new questions.
- "Raise the confidence cutoff so that more goes to the frontier model." That buys quality back at a cost without finding the cause. Retrain the router and gate it online.

questions.title: Break an eight-minute start into its parts
questions.prompt: A pod serving an MoE model on a unified-memory machine took about eight minutes from start to ready. Break that time into its parts, say which parts a restart can skip, and estimate what a warm restart looks like on the same machine.
questions.short: Most of the time was the weight load. The manual's log shows about 330 seconds to copy 57 GiB of weights into memory on that machine, one tensor at a time from a file-backed page. The engine init took 127.54 seconds, and it holds the two CUDA graph captures of 39 and 38 seconds and a compile share of 18.67 seconds. A restart reuses the compile cache and nothing else, so a warm restart on that machine is only a little shorter than the cold one, unless the weights are staged in host memory or a process snapshot exists, which a field report took from a cold start of 695 seconds to 9.6 seconds.
questions.full:
### The parts, from the startup log

| Phase | Measured | Where it is logged |
|---|---|---|
| weight load | 56.93 GiB in about 330 seconds | the model loading line |
| engine init, profile, KV cache, warmup, with both graph captures | 127.54 seconds, of which compilation 18.67 | the init engine line |
| first graph capture, inside engine init | 39 seconds, 1.17 GiB | the first graph capturing line |
| second graph capture, inside engine init | 38 seconds, 0.31 GiB | the second graph capturing line |

The two captures finish before the init line, so they are part of its 127.54 seconds. Do not add them to it.

The server reported ready about eight minutes after it read its arguments. The load alone is more than two thirds of it.

### Why the load is slow on this machine

Each tensor is copied from the memory-mapped weights file into the GPU allocation. On this platform an open issue measured about 1.7 ms per tensor copied from the file view, against about 0.2 ms for a copy that starts in host memory. The release that the manual pins saved about 25 seconds with an indexed lookup of expert names, and the per-tensor copy cost stays. The manual's advice: keep the weights on local NVMe, not on a network mount, and start the server once and keep it running.

### What a restart skips

The compile cache lives under the engine's cache directory. Keep it on a persistent volume, and a later start reads it, so the compile share shrinks. SGLang points all of its kernel caches into one directory for the same reason, and the manual mounts it on a volume that survives the pod. The graph captures and the weight load repeat on every start. So the honest estimate for a warm restart on this machine is the cold start minus the compile share, which is still several minutes.

### Getting under a minute

The lesson on cold starts maps each phase to a layer: a pre-seeded image removes the image pull, model streaming roughly halves the weight load, and a GPU memory snapshot restores the loaded state about ten times faster than a reload. The SGLang manual quotes a field report with the same shape on a different engine and eight GPUs: a cold start of 695 seconds with 531 of them in weight loading, 88 seconds with kernel caches kept, and 9.6 seconds with a process checkpoint and the weights staged in host memory. Below a minute means a snapshot or staged weights, not a faster disk.

### What the number sets

The Kubernetes example in the vLLM manual gives the startup probe checks at 10 second intervals across a 15 minute window, and tells you to set the window from your own measured cold start. An autoscaler needs a stabilization window at least as long, and the interactive path needs a warm replica, because no scale-out helps inside an eight-minute window.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Which phase dominates on this machine, and why? Expected: the weight load at about 330 seconds, because each tensor is copied from a file-backed page, which is slow on this platform.
- **Level 3:** What does a persistent compile cache save on a restart? Expected: the compile share of the engine init, 18.67 seconds here. The weight load and the graph captures remain.
- **Level 4:** How do you get the restart under a minute? Expected: a process checkpoint or GPU memory snapshot with the weights staged in host memory, which the field report took to 9.6 seconds. A faster disk alone does not get there.
- **Level 4:** What does an eight-minute start imply for the probes and the autoscaler? Expected: a startup probe window longer than eight minutes, a stabilization window at least as long, and a warm replica for the interactive path.
questions.wrong:
- "The compile is the slow part, use eager mode." The compile share was 18.67 seconds of an eight-minute start, and eager mode costs decode speed on every request afterwards.
- "A faster GPU loads faster." The load was bound by the copy path from the file view, not by the GPU.
- "Restart often to pick up configuration changes." Each restart pays the full load. The manual's advice is to start once and keep the server running.

questions.title: Build a cost attribution and enforcement simulator
questions.prompt: Take-home. You receive one day of request logs from a multi-tenant assistant. Each record follows the lesson's attribution trace: a trace id, a timestamp, the tenant, the user, the task id and its route, the model, the token counts for each of the four layers in the lesson's trace, whether the input was cached, and whether the task was resolved. You also receive the daily spend of each tenant over the previous weeks, as the baseline for the kill switch. Build a simulator that attributes spend by tenant, task and user, splits the tokens into layers, computes a cost per resolved task per tenant, and enforces a rate limit, a daily spend cap and a kill switch. Inject one abusive tenant and show when each control fires.
questions.short: Price every call from a pricing table, roll the cost up by tenant, by task with its route and by user, and split the tokens into prompt, tool, memory and response so that the report names the layer that drives each tenant's spend. Compute the cost per resolved task from the outcome field, not from the token totals. Implement the ladder from the lesson: a rate limit at 2 to 3 times the expected peak, a daily cap at 1.5 to 3 times the contracted ceiling, and a kill switch on a spend z-score above 4 against the tenant's own baseline. Show the abusive tenant hit the rate limit first, then the cap, then the kill switch when its spend jumps far above its history.
questions.full:
### What a complete submission contains

1. **A cost on every call.** A pricing table with the cached input price, as the earlier caching lesson builds it, and a function that turns tokens into dollars per call.
2. **Attribution in three dimensions.** Spend by tenant, by task and route, and by user, joined by the trace id as the telemetry joiner pattern does. Nothing is inferred after the fact.
3. **Four token layers.** Prompt, tool, memory and response per task, as shares. The lesson's typical bands are the sanity check: prompt 40 to 60 percent, tool 20 to 40 percent on agent work, memory and response 10 to 30 percent each.
4. **The unit metric.** For every tenant and every feature, the spend divided by the resolved tasks, from the resolution field. A task that was not resolved still cost money, and that is the point of the metric.
5. **The enforcement ladder.** The rate limit answers with a 429 and a retry header. The cap tightens the rate limit and raises an alert. The kill switch pauses the tenant and pages.
6. **The injected tenant.** A timeline of its spend and of the control that fired at each point, with the z-score plotted against the threshold.
7. **The first five dashboard views.** The lesson's exercise asks for them. A strong answer: spend per tenant over time, the per-tenant spend divided by resolved tasks, the layer split per task, the top users by spend, and the enforcement events.

### What the reviewer looks for

- The attribution is stamped at request creation and joined by trace id, never guessed from the bill.
- The layers are separate, and the report says which one to fix for each heavy tenant.
- The unit metric is tied to an outcome.
- The kill switch is relative to the tenant's own baseline, and the threshold is justified, which is the lesson's first exercise.
- The order of the controls is explained: friction first, pause last.

### What to argue in the write-up

The lesson's third exercise: the largest tenant has a negative margin. Propose three interventions ordered by customer impact, such as caching and routing on their heaviest task first, a quota change second, and a price change at renewal last. Then argue whether retroactive tagging can ever work, which the lesson asks in its last exercise. The honest answer is that it fills a gap for legacy data and always misses cases.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why is the kill switch relative to each tenant's history instead of a fixed amount? Expected: tenants differ by orders of magnitude. A fixed amount pauses a large tenant on a normal day and never fires for a small one.
- **Level 4:** Your largest tenant is unprofitable in the report. What do you propose? Expected: three interventions ordered by customer impact, such as caching and routing on their heaviest task, then a quota change, then a price change at renewal.
- **Level 4:** Which five views would you put on the dashboard first? Expected: spend per tenant over time, the per-tenant spend divided by resolved tasks, the layer split per task, the top users by spend, and the enforcement events timeline.
questions.wrong:
- "Attribute the bill by dividing it by seats." That hides the heavy tenants and the heavy features, which is what the exercise is for.
- "One token bucket for everything." A single bucket cannot say which layer or tenant to fix, and it cannot carry a per-tenant cap.
- "Fire the kill switch at a fixed dollar amount." Tenants differ by orders of magnitude. A fixed amount is wrong for all but one of them.

questions.title: The metric to give finance instead of a token price
questions.prompt: Finance asks for the cost per million tokens as the key metric for the model service. You push back. What metric do you propose instead, and what must every call record so that you can compute it?
questions.short: Propose a cost per product outcome: per resolved ticket, per generated article, per successful agent task or per session minute. A price per million tokens is the vendor's unit, and it says nothing about whether the spend produced anything. To compute the outcome metric, stamp every call at creation with the user id, the task id with its route, and the tenant id, split the tokens into prompt, tool, memory and response, and join the cost to the outcome event.
questions.full:
### Why the token price misleads

A cheaper model that needs twice the tokens per task costs more per task. A prompt change that cuts tokens and lowers the resolution rate raises the cost per resolved ticket while the token dashboard goes green. The lesson's rule is to tie cost to a product outcome, because an optimization without that anchor has no direction.

### Three attribution dimensions

| Dimension | Key | What it answers |
|---|---|---|
| per user | `user_id` | who costs what, for seat pricing and abuse |
| per task | `task_id` and `route` | which product surface costs what |
| per tenant | `tenant_id` | which customer is profitable |

Instrument all three at the call site on day one. A provider line item carries none of them, and retroactive tagging always misses cases.

### Four token layers

| Layer | Typical share |
|---|---|
| prompt, the system text and the user input | 40 to 60 percent |
| tool, the results fed back into the context | 20 to 40 percent on agent workloads |
| memory, the prior turns and retrieved documents | 10 to 30 percent |
| response, the model output | 10 to 30 percent |

One bucket hides which layer drives the spend, so you cannot pick the lever.

### The record on every call

The trace carries the trace id, the three dimension keys, the four layer counts, the cost, and two flags, one for a cached input and one for a batch call. The most accurate attribution pattern joins these traces to the billing export by trace id, which the lesson calls the telemetry joiner.
questions.followups:
- **Level 1:** Why does the token price alone mislead? Expected: it says nothing about tokens per outcome. A cheaper model that needs twice the tokens per task costs more per task.
- **Level 2:** Why split the tokens into four layers? Expected: one bucket hides whether prompt bloat, tool results, memory or output drives the spend, so you cannot choose the right fix.
- **Level 2:** Why stamp the call at creation instead of tagging the bill later? Expected: the provider line item has no user, task or tenant on it, and retroactive attribution always misses cases.
- **Level 3:** Which attribution pattern is the most accurate, and what does it need? Expected: the telemetry joiner, which joins trace ids to billing. It needs the trace id on every call and a billing export with the same key.
questions.wrong:
- "Tokens are what we pay for, so tokens are the metric." They are the vendor's unit. The business pays for outcomes, and a cheaper token can mean a more expensive task.
- "Tag the cloud bill by team like any other resource." A model call is a transaction, not an asset. The line item has no team on it unless the call stamped one.
- "Per-tenant cost is enough." Per-task shows which feature to fix and per-user shows abuse. The lesson instruments all three.

questions.title: Read the exact-match cache before it ships
questions.short: The cache serves deterministic calls only. A positive temperature asks for sampled variation, and a replayed answer would remove that variation without telling the caller, so the cache treats those calls as misses and never stores them. The key is a hash of the model, the full message list and the temperature, serialized with sorted keys so that the same request always produces the same bytes. Before production, the key needs every other field that changes the answer, the eviction needs a least-recently-used policy instead of a full scan for the oldest entry, and the expiry needs a sweep, because an expired entry is only removed when someone reads it.
questions.full:
### The temperature guard

Both `get` and `put` return early above zero. The lesson's rule is that exact caching works for deterministic calls: the same model, the same prompt, temperature zero. Serving a stored sample to a caller who asked for variation changes the behavior silently, which is worse than a miss.

### What the key holds, and what it misses

The key covers the model, because the same prompt on another model is another answer, the whole message list, because the system prompt and the context are part of the request, and the temperature. `sort_keys=True` makes the serialization stable, so two callers who build the same dictionary in a different order still hash alike. The key does not cover other fields that change the answer: the sampling parameters beyond temperature, the output limit, the tool definitions and the response format. Add them, or the cache returns an answer produced under different settings.

### Expiry is lazy

The lifetime is checked on read. An entry past its lifetime stays in memory until a read finds it or an eviction drops it. A periodic sweep, or an expiry check during `put`, keeps the memory honest.

### Eviction is a full scan, oldest first

At capacity, `put` scans every entry to find the oldest timestamp. That is linear work on every insert once the cache is full, and it evicts by insertion time, so a popular entry that was inserted early goes first. The lesson's first exercise asks for least-recently-used eviction on the last access time, which the `access_count` field hints at but does not implement.

### Prove that it pays

The cache counts hits and misses. The lesson's cost tracker logs a cache status on every call and computes the saved cost from the hits with the pricing table. Wire that in before you argue about the hit rate.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why serialize with sorted keys? Expected: the order of a dictionary can differ between callers, and a different byte order gives a different hash for the same request.
- **Level 3:** Which request fields are missing from the key? Expected: anything else that changes the answer, such as the other sampling parameters, the output limit, the tool definitions and the response format.
- **Level 3:** What does the eviction do at capacity, and what does the exercise ask for instead? Expected: it scans all entries for the oldest timestamp and drops it. The exercise asks for least-recently-used eviction on the last access time.
- **Level 4:** How would you show that this cache pays for itself? Expected: log the cache status on every call and compute the saved cost from the hits with the pricing table, as the lesson's cost tracker does.
questions.wrong:
- "The temperature check is pointless, a cached answer is a good answer." A positive temperature means the caller wants variation. A replay removes it without telling anyone.
- "Hash only the user message." The same question under a different system prompt, model or tool set has a different correct answer.
- "The lifetime removes expired entries." It only hides them on read. The entry stays in memory until a read or an eviction removes it.

questions.title: Which gateways fit in a 20 ms tail budget
questions.prompt: Your SLA is a P99 time to first token under 320 ms. The model alone measures 300 ms at P99. You are choosing a gateway to put in front of it. Which classes of gateway fit in the budget, and what do you do when the one you want does not?
questions.short: The gateway has at most 20 ms at the tail. An edge-managed gateway at 1 to 3 ms and a high-performance gateway at 3 to 8 ms fit, a lightweight proxy at 5 to 15 ms fits with little margin, and a control-plane gateway at 20 to 40 ms does not. If you need the features of the slow one, split the roles: keep the fast gateway on the request path, run the heavy features out of band, or buy the budget back from the model with a faster first token.
questions.full:
### The budget

The target is 320 ms and the model takes 300 ms, so the gateway may add 20 ms, and that is at the tail. A P99 target means the gateway's own P99, not its median, and a gateway that is quick when idle can be slow under load. The sum of the two tails is a screening estimate only. Before you commit to the SLA, measure the end-to-end first-token P99 through the gateway under load.

### The classes

| Class | Overhead in the lesson | Fits |
|---|---|---|
| edge-managed, zero-ops | 1 to 3 ms | yes |
| high-performance, built on a mature API gateway | 3 to 8 ms | yes |
| lightweight open-source proxy | 5 to 15 ms | with little margin |
| control plane with guardrails and audit | 20 to 40 ms | no |

The lesson's rule of thumb matches: for a P99 under 100 ms, pick the edge or the high-performance class. For a P99 under 500 ms, any class works.

### When you want the slow one

The control-plane class brings PII redaction, jailbreak detection and audit trails. Three ways to keep them inside the budget:

1. Split the roles. Put the fast gateway on the request path and run observability and audit off the path. The lesson notes that production deployments combine an observability tool with a scale gateway in exactly this split.
2. Keep only what must be inline. Redaction has to run before the provider sees the prompt, so it stays on the path. Audit and tracing do not.
3. Buy back budget from the model. Prefix caching lowers the first-token time, and a faster model tier does too.

### Scale decides as well

The lightweight proxy breaks down around 2000 requests per second with an 8 GB footprint in the published benchmark, and the lesson places it below 500 requests per second. If the traffic will grow past that, the high-performance class is the only one that fits both the latency and the scale.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why measure the gateway at P99 and not at its median? Expected: the SLA is a P99, and the gateway's tail adds to the model's tail.
- **Level 3:** The slow gateway's value is PII redaction. How do you keep it inside the budget? Expected: keep the redaction inline because it must run before the provider sees the prompt, move observability and audit off the path, and then measure whether the remaining overhead fits.
- **Level 3:** Traffic will triple next year. Which class survives? Expected: the lightweight proxy breaks down around 2000 requests per second, so plan the move to the high-performance class before that.
questions.wrong:
- "Every gateway adds a few milliseconds, pick on features." The lesson's overheads run from 1 to 40 ms, and 40 ms is twice this budget.
- "Put the gateway behind the model, not in front." The gateway routes and falls back before the model. Behind the model it protects nothing.
- "Add the gateway's median to the model's P99." Two tails do not add that way. Measure the gateway's own tail under load.

questions.title: Two cache hit rates from one scrape
questions.prompt: A dashboard panel shows the prefix cache hit rate of a self-hosted server at 94 percent. Over the same run, the server's counters say that it computed 104,057 prompt tokens and took 182,079 from the cache. Both readings come from one scrape of the same endpoint. Which one do you trust for a cost decision, and why do they differ?
questions.short: Trust the counters. The gauge holds the hit rate of the last prefill interval that the scheduler logged, and at idle it keeps the value from the last batch, which was a shared-prefix benchmark. The counters add up every prefill token since the server started, and their ratio over the whole run is 0.636, not 0.942. For a cost decision, compute the rate from the counters over a time window.
questions.full:
### Three kinds of series

A gauge is a value the scheduler overwrites on each log interval. A scrape sees the latest value only. A counter is a total that only grows, and you read it as a rate over a window. A histogram is a set of counters, one per bucket, and you read percentiles from it over a window.

### The two hit rates

The gauge divides the hit tokens of one log interval by the hit tokens plus the computed tokens of that interval. When nothing runs, it keeps its last value. The counters carry the same two quantities since startup, split by mode: input for computed tokens, and device, host and storage hits for cached tokens. Over the whole run, 182,079 cached tokens against 286,136 prefill tokens in total give 0.636. The gauge at 0.942 describes the shared-prefix benchmark that ran last. Both are correct, and they answer different questions.

### The windowed rate

The HELP text of the counter gives the formula, and in PromQL it reads:

```promql
sum(rate(sglang:prefill_effective_tokens_total{mode=~".*_hit"}[5m]))
  / sum(rate(sglang:prefill_effective_tokens_total[5m]))
```

One caveat from the code: the hit modes add raw hit counts, so after a retraction the same tokens can count twice. The input mode excludes the re-count. The manual's run had no retractions, so its numbers are exact.

### Why this is a cost question

A hit rate decides whether you restructure prompts, add a cache-aware router or buy memory. A gauge from the last benchmark says the prompts are fine. The counters say that more than a third of the prompt tokens over the run were computed. The lesson on caching economics says the same for provider caches: measure your own hit rate from the usage fields on every response, and do not take a published figure as yours.

### What to alert on

Alert on counters and histograms over a window. Alert on a gauge only when the condition lasts for several minutes, such as queued requests above zero or token usage near one. Read the HELP text and the code before you build a panel on a metric. The manual found one utilization gauge that stays at zero at the version it pinned.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** What does a gauge answer, and what does a counter answer? Expected: a gauge answers what happened in the last interval. A counter answers how much happened since the start, and a rate over a window turns it into a trend.
- **Level 3:** Why can the counter-based rate overstate the hits after retractions? Expected: the hit modes add raw hit counts, so a retracted request that runs again counts its cached tokens twice, while the input mode excludes the re-count.
- **Level 3:** Which gauges may page you, and under what rule? Expected: queued requests above zero and token usage near one, only when the condition holds for several minutes, never on one scrape.
- **Level 4:** A panel on this server shows utilization at zero during an outage. Why? Expected: that gauge stays at zero at the pinned version because of a known regression, so the panel shows an idle fleet. Read the HELP text and the code before building on a metric.
questions.wrong:
- "The gauge is the newest value, so it is the most accurate." It is a snapshot of one interval, and it keeps its last value at idle.
- "Average the two numbers." They answer different questions, and the counters already contain the whole run.
- "The real rate is lower, so turn the cache off." A rate of 0.636 means a third of the prompt tokens were computed. The fix is the prompt layout or the routing, not the cache.

questions.title: A few endless answers fill the pool for everyone
questions.prompt: A self-hosted server shows its KV pool near full for hours while the request rate is normal. A few requests have been generating for many minutes each, and the users behind the other requests wait. What is going on, and what do you change tonight and tomorrow?
questions.short: A handful of requests are in a generation loop. Every token of a running request stays in the pool until the request ends, so a request that never stops grows until it crowds out the rest. Tonight, cap the output length so that every request ends, and add a presence penalty for the workloads that loop. Tomorrow, set the shutdown grace period from the new cap, because a request that runs to the cap decides how long a graceful restart takes.
questions.full:
### The mechanism

The pool holds the keys and values of every token of every running request. A request in a loop keeps generating, so it keeps taking slots until it reaches the output limit or the context length. With no cap, one looping request can hold a large share of the pool for the whole context, and new requests wait or running ones are retracted.

### A production report with the same shape

The SGLang manual summarizes an academic service that served a hundred billion tokens and ran into model loops that held KV cache. Their traffic came from agentic coding tools, with a median prompt of 2,179 tokens and a 95th percentile of 99,746 tokens. Their fix was operational, not a kernel: an output cap of 32K tokens and a presence penalty for the workloads that loop. The manual's advice is to read such a report for its order of fixes, and that service capped output before it tuned anything else.

### Read the metrics

The vLLM manual's alert table has the pattern: cache usage above 0.95 for more than a minute, waiting requests above zero, and a preemption rate above zero. Its pairing rule names the cause: preemptions with long answers mean that running requests grow until the pool runs out. The fixes it lists are lower concurrency or an FP8 KV cache, and the output cap is what turns the long answers into bounded ones.

### Why the cap comes before the grace period

A graceful shutdown drains the running requests before it stops. The grace period has to outlast the longest request, and the longest request is one that runs to the cap. The SGLang manual's arithmetic: an answer of 32K tokens at 30 tokens per second needs more than 18 minutes. Cap the output first, then set the termination grace period from the cap, or a drain can never finish in time and a rolling update kills requests mid-answer.

### Tomorrow

- Find the loops: requests that finished with the length reason at the cap, grouped by tenant and prompt template.
- Set per-tenant output caps that the product agreed to.
- If the long answers turn out to be real agent sessions, grow the pool with an FP8 KV cache or more memory, and lower the concurrency cap.
- Alert on the pair: cache usage near one with a normal request rate.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why does a looping request hurt other users and not only itself? Expected: the pool is shared. A request that never ends keeps its slots, so new requests wait or running ones are retracted.
- **Level 3:** How do you find the looping requests after the fact? Expected: requests that finished with the length reason at the cap, grouped by tenant and prompt template.
- **Level 4:** Why does the cap on output length come first, before you pick how long a drain may take? Expected: the grace period must outlast the longest request, and the longest request runs to the cap. The manual's arithmetic gives more than 18 minutes for 32K tokens at 30 tokens per second.
- **Level 4:** The long answers are legitimate agent sessions. What then? Expected: grow the pool with an FP8 KV cache or more memory, lower the concurrency cap, and keep an output cap that the product agreed to.
questions.wrong:
- "Restart the server to clear the pool." Every running request fails, and the loops come back on the next prompt.
- "Raise the memory fraction." A larger pool delays the symptom. A request with no cap fills any pool.
- "Lower the temperature to stop the loops." Sampling settings change the odds of a loop. Only a cap guarantees that a request ends.

questions.title: Price a nightly pipeline on batch with a cached prompt
questions.prompt: A nightly pipeline summarizes 50,000 documents, and every call opens with the same system prompt. It runs synchronously against a provider for four hours and costs about 2,000 dollars a night. Estimate what the same job costs on the batch API with the system prompt cached, and say when you would move it onto your own GPU instead.
questions.short: Batch gives a flat 50 percent discount on input and output tokens, and the cached system prompt makes the repeated input about ten times cheaper after the first write. Stacked, the lesson's worked example lands at about 180 dollars a night, near 9 percent of the synchronous bill, from three configuration changes. Move the job to your own GPU when it runs every night at high utilization and the shared prefix is short, so that neither discount has much to work on, and size that run by raising concurrency until the output stops growing.
questions.full:
### The three bills

The lesson writes the synchronous uncached bill as the document count times the input and output tokens of each call at full rates, with a shared prompt of about 4000 tokens and an output of about 200 tokens per document.

1. **Synchronous, uncached.** Every call pays for the full prompt and the full output.
2. **Synchronous, cached.** The system prompt is written once, and the remaining 49999 calls read it at about a tenth of the input price.
3. **Batch, cached.** Everything above, plus the 50 percent discount on the reads, the write and the output.

The lesson's conclusion: batch plus cache comes to about 10 percent of the synchronous uncached bill, and its worked pipeline goes from 2,000 dollars a night to about 180.

### What the estimate hides

- Output tokens take the batch discount only. Caching reuses the prompt's attention state and does nothing for generated tokens, so a job with long outputs and a short prompt saves much less.
- The first call of a batch pays the cache write premium. Against tens of thousands of reads, it is noise. If the batch runs longer than the cache lifetime, the one-hour variant with its 2x write is worth it once the reads pass five.
- Check the usage fields on a sample of the results. A batch whose requests all missed the cache shows writes and no reads, and then the second discount never happened.
- The return is promised within 24 hours and typical within a few hours. A night is shorter than the promise, so the morning deadline holds only on the typical return. Submit the batch a day ahead, or keep a synchronous fallback for a late batch.

### When your own GPU wins

The lesson's exercise asks for the shared-prefix length at which batch plus cache beats a reserved GPU running overnight. Your own GPU wins when three things hold: the job keeps a reserved GPU busy every night, the shared prefix is short, so there is little to cache, and the outputs are long, so the batch discount is the only lever on the provider side. Data residency can decide it on its own.

### How to size the self-hosted run

The vLLM manual's recipe for an offline job: pass the whole prompt list to the offline engine class in one call, or run the batch command on a file of requests, and raise the concurrency until the output stops growing. On its card, the output grew to 273.9 tokens per second at 32 concurrent requests and fell to 241.4 at 64, because the pool filled and the GPU throttled. Raise the token budget above 8,192 for throughput, because a slow first token costs nothing when nobody waits, and watch the running count against the cache usage to see which limit binds.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Which of the two discounts applies to output tokens? Expected: only the batch discount. Caching lowers the price of repeated input and does nothing for generated tokens.
- **Level 3:** The first call in each batch pays a cache write premium. Does that change the estimate? Expected: not at this volume. One write at a quarter more, against tens of thousands of reads at a tenth of the price.
- **Level 4:** When does a reserved GPU beat batch plus cache? Expected: when the job keeps the GPU busy every night, the shared prefix is short and the outputs are long, so the two discounts have little to work on. The lesson's exercise computes the break-even prefix length.
- **Level 4:** How do you find the right concurrency for the job on your own GPU? Expected: pass the whole list to the offline engine or the batch command, raise concurrency until the output tokens per second stop growing, and raise the token budget. The manual's card peaked near 32 concurrent requests.
questions.wrong:
- "Batch alone gets you to a tenth of the cost." Batch alone halves the bill. The other factor is the cached shared prompt.
- "Caching saves the same on output as on input." The cache reuses the prompt's attention state. Every output token is generated and billed in full, less the batch discount.
- "Batch is too slow for a nightly job." The promise is a day and the typical return is hours. Submit a day ahead, or keep a synchronous fallback for the rare late batch.

questions.title: Ten parallel tool calls, ten cache writes, no reads
questions.prompt: An agent fans out ten tool calls at once for every user question. All ten share the same long system prompt, and prompt caching is on. The bill is several times what the cache should allow, and the usage fields show cache writes on nearly all calls and almost no cache reads. What is happening?
questions.short: All ten requests reach the provider before the first one has finished writing the prefix into the cache. Each one sees a miss, each one pays the write premium, and none of them reads. The fix is sequential-first: send one request alone, let its cache write land, then fan out the other nine. It adds about one write latency to the first tool call and removes the inflation.
questions.full:
### The mechanism

Cache writes happen per request. The lesson puts the first write at about 300 ms after the provider sees the prompt. Requests that arrive inside that window find nothing to read, so each of them writes. Ten writes and zero reads, on every user question that finds the prefix cold. A question that arrives while an earlier write is still inside the cache lifetime reads it, so the trap shows when the questions are further apart than that lifetime. The lesson reports a bill of 5 to 10 times the expected cached cost from this pattern alone.

### Read the usage fields

Each response reports the tokens written to the cache and the tokens read from it. In this incident the written count is high on every request and the read count is near zero. That is the signature. A later sequential request with the same prefix does read, which separates this case from a prefix that never matches.

### The fix

Send the first request alone and wait for it to return. Its write has landed by then. Fan out the remaining nine, and each of them reads. The cost is about 300 ms on the first tool call. The lesson's exercise asks for the same fix without adding end-to-end latency: warm the prefix with one call at the start of the session, before the first fan-out, so the first tool call already reads.

### Rule out the other cause

A prefix that carries dynamic text looks the same in the usage fields: writes on every request, no reads ever. The lesson's example has the time to the minute, a user id and a reshuffled example order inside the system prompt. One field report moved the hit rate from 7 to 74 percent by moving that text below the cache boundary. Check the prompt template before you blame the fan-out.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** How do you tell the fan-out trap from dynamic text in the prefix? Expected: both show writes and no reads. After the fan-out trap, a later sequential request with the same prefix reads. With dynamic text, nothing ever reads.
- **Level 3:** How do you fix the fan-out without adding latency for the user? Expected: warm the prefix with one call when the session starts, so the first fan-out already reads.
- **Level 3:** Does a self-hosted prefix cache have the same trap? Expected: the lesson says the self-hosted caches follow the same prefix pattern at your own compute, so measure the cached tokens on a fan-out before you assume they are shared.
questions.wrong:
- "Caching is on, so the provider should deduplicate them." Writes are per request, and the cache can be read only after the first write has landed.
- "Shorten the system prompt." That lowers every bill a little and leaves ten writes and zero reads in place.
- "Turn caching off, it costs more." It costs more only because of the arrival pattern. Sequential-first turns ten writes into one write and nine reads.

questions.title: Per-token or per-minute billing for a daytime load
questions.prompt: Two inference platforms quote you for the same open model. One bills per million tokens. The other rents a dedicated GPU by the minute. Your traffic is steady through the working day and near zero at night. Which pricing wins, and what number decides it?
questions.short: Sustained utilization decides it. Per-token billing charges only for what you use, so it wins when traffic is bursty or low and a dedicated GPU would sit idle. Per-minute billing charges for wall-clock time, so it wins once you keep the GPU busy, and the lesson's rule of thumb puts the crossover near 30 percent sustained utilization. A load that runs only in the daytime sits near that line, so measure your utilization over a full week before you sign.
questions.full:
### Two cost functions for one output

Per-token pricing reflects the platform's own utilization curve across all of its customers, and you pay for no idle time. Per-minute or per-second pricing reflects exclusivity: the GPU is yours, and the bill runs whether or not a request arrives. The output, a model response, is the same.

### The crossover

The economics lesson states the rule: above about 30 percent sustained utilization of a dedicated GPU, per-minute starts to beat per-token. Below it, per-token wins because you are not paying for idle. The lesson on managed platforms shows the same shape for reserved capacity on a hyperscaler: the break-even sits around 40 to 60 percent sustained utilization, savings reach up to 70 percent at high utilization, and the reservation is billed when idle.

### Compute it for your own traffic

1. Take the request count per hour of the day for a week, and the tokens per request.
2. The per-token bill is the token total times the rate.
3. The per-minute bill is the rented hours times the rate. That is every hour unless you scale to zero at night, which brings a cold start every morning.
4. Utilization is the busy time divided by the rented time. Compare it with the crossover.

### What the price does not show

- Dedicated capacity avoids queueing behind other tenants. The lesson on managed platforms measures a lower first-token median on reserved capacity than on shared on-demand for the same model class.
- A fine-tuned model can change the per-token price. One platform in the lesson serves a fine-tune at the base model's rate, which is a differentiator. A dedicated GPU serves it at the same hourly price either way.
- Non-interactive work has a third option: a batch tier at about half the serverless rate.

### A mixed answer

Rent dedicated capacity for the daytime floor, and send the overflow and the overnight batch to per-token or batch pricing. The utilization of the dedicated part then stays high, and the bursts never pay for an idle GPU.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why does per-token pricing cost more per token than your own GPU time at high utilization? Expected: the platform's margin and its idle time are built into the per-token rate. At high utilization you pay for idle that you do not have.
- **Level 2:** What changes when you scale the dedicated GPU to zero at night? Expected: you stop paying for the night and buy a cold start every morning, so the first requests of the day pay in latency.
- **Level 3:** Why is the dedicated option faster at the tail? Expected: shared on-demand capacity competes with every other customer's traffic, and dedicated capacity does not. That is the gap the lesson on managed platforms measures between reserved and on-demand first-token latency.
- **Level 3:** How does a fine-tuned model change the comparison? Expected: a per-token platform may serve the fine-tune at the base rate or charge a premium for it. A dedicated GPU serves it at the same hourly price either way.
questions.wrong:
- "Per-token is always cheaper because you never pay for idle." Above the utilization crossover, the per-token rate carries the platform's idle and margin, and your own GPU is cheaper.
- "Dedicated is always cheaper at scale." Only when you keep it busy. A daytime-only load leaves it idle half the time.
- "Compare the headline prices." The two prices have different units. Only your traffic profile turns them into a bill.

questions.title: A second replica that undoes the prefix cache
questions.prompt: You add a second serving replica to double capacity. Throughput rises, but the first-token time of long chat sessions gets worse, and the cache hit rate on both servers falls. Explain the cause, and design the routing so that the second replica stops undoing the cache.
questions.short: Each replica has its own KV cache, and a router that spreads requests at random or in turn sends turn five of a chat to the replica that never saw turns one to four. That replica prefills the whole history again, which is the prefix miss the cache exists to avoid. Route each conversation back to the replica that holds its prefix with a cache-aware policy that remembers which server saw which text, with a load-balance check in front of it. Then read the hit rate on the servers themselves, because the router's record is a guess.
questions.full:
### The mechanism

A plain Kubernetes Service spreads requests at random. The in-server data parallel controller of SGLang defaults to round robin, which ignores prefixes. Either way, a conversation's turns land on different replicas, and each replica computes the history that the other one already holds. A field report in the SGLang manual measured the damage: with turn-by-turn routing, 23 percent of input tokens were computed again. One request header that pinned each conversation to one GPU raised the cache hit rate from 64.7 to 92.1 percent and halved the median time to first token.

### How a cache-aware router picks a server

The SGLang gateway keeps one approximate radix tree per model, over the characters of the request text, so it never tokenizes to route. For each request it does three things in order:

1. It checks balance. When the busiest server's load is more than 64 above the lightest and more than 1.5 times the lightest, the request goes to the least-loaded server.
2. Otherwise it computes the match rate, the share of the request text that matches the tree. Above 0.3, the request goes to the server with the longest match.
3. Below 0.3, it goes to the least-loaded server.

Every 120 seconds a background task trims each tree to at most 67,108,864 nodes. The balance check comes first on purpose: a prefix-first policy would pile every long conversation onto one hot server.

### The tree is a guess

The gateway records where it sent text. It never asks a server what it still holds, and a server can evict the prefix later. So a request can arrive at the server the tree names and still prefill. Check the hit rate on the servers themselves, from their counters over a window, and not only the routing decisions.

### Pick the policy by traffic

Cache-aware routing for chat and agent traffic, where turns share long prefixes. A power-of-two or round-robin policy for batch traffic with unique prompts, because a match rate under the threshold gives no affinity anyway. Do not put multi-turn traffic behind in-server data parallelism with its round-robin default.

### The same idea in the vLLM layers

The vLLM manual lists routers that read the engine's metrics to pick a replica, and one that also reads the KV cache events the engine publishes with `--kv-events-config`, so that a request goes to the replica that holds its prefix. The production stack's router keeps a session on one replica. In the gateway lesson's vocabulary, this is provider routing one level down: the AI gateway routes across providers, and the engine router routes across replicas.

### Pin the router with the engine

The SGLang manual records an incident where the same engine build gave 132,140 tokens per second with one router version and 69,767 with the next. Benchmark the router and the engine as one system, and pin both versions.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why does the router check load balance before the prefix match? Expected: a prefix-first policy would send every long conversation to one hot server. The imbalance test sends the request to the least-loaded server when the gap is large.
- **Level 3:** Which traffic should not use the cache-aware policy? Expected: batch traffic with unique prompts. A match rate under the threshold gives no affinity, so a load-based policy does the same work with less state.
- **Level 4:** One server's hit rate stays low although the gateway routes its conversations there. Why? Expected: the gateway's tree records where it sent text, not what the server still holds. The server evicted the prefix, so the request prefills. Read the server's own counters.
- **Level 4:** You upgrade the router without touching the engine. What do you measure? Expected: throughput and hit rate of the router and the engine as one system, because a router change alone halved throughput in a reported incident.
questions.wrong:
- "Add a replica and each server's hit rate stays the same." Each replica has its own cache, and random routing splits every conversation across both.
- "Hash the user id to a server and be done." It keeps a user on one server and ignores load. The manual's gateway balances first, so a hot user cannot saturate one replica with no relief.
- "Turn on in-server data parallelism instead of a gateway." Its default method is round robin, which ignores prefixes, which is the problem you are solving.

questions.title: Warm replicas per tier, with the arithmetic
questions.prompt: You run three tiers on a serverless GPU platform: paid users on a live chat, trial users on the same chat, and a nightly batch pipeline. Design the warm-pool policy per tier, show the arithmetic behind it, and say what you would measure after a month to revisit it.
questions.short: Give the paid chat one or two warm replicas, because its first-token target cannot absorb a cold start of minutes on a large model. Give trial users a smaller margin, or let them ride on the paid pool's spare capacity, and let the batch pipeline scale to zero, because it tolerates a cold start of several minutes. The arithmetic is the hourly GPU price times the idle hours against the requests that would miss the target during a cold start, and after a month you compare the measured utilization, the cold-start count and the missed-target count per tier.
questions.full:
### The arithmetic the lesson gives

A warm replica costs one GPU hour every hour. One replica per product is a full month of GPU hours whether anyone calls, and the lesson's example of five products with one warm replica each comes to 3,600 GPU-hours a month idle. The lesson calls the trade brutal on small models, where you pay 0.85 to 1.50 dollars an hour to avoid a 30 second start, and kind on large ones, where about 4 dollars an hour avoids a 5 minute start. Its threshold for a mandatory warm pool: a first-token target at P99 under 60 seconds on a model of 70B or more.

### The policy per tier

| Tier | Policy | Why |
|---|---|---|
| paid live chat | one to two warm replicas | the lesson's high-value interactive path, where a cold start is an outage |
| trial chat | zero warm, or overflow into the paid pool at lower priority | the loss is a conversion, which you can measure, against a month of GPU hours |
| nightly batch | scale to zero | the lesson accepts a cold start of 5 to 10 minutes on background paths |

The lesson's exercise asks exactly this split and asks for the math. The paid tier is decided by the SLA. The batch tier is decided by its tolerance. The trial tier is the real decision, and it is an experiment: the conversion loss from a cold start on the first session against the price of an idle GPU.

### Make the policy cheaper by shrinking the start

Every mitigation layer moves a tier toward zero. A pre-seeded node image removes the image pull, model streaming halves the weight load, a GPU memory snapshot restores the loaded state in a fraction of the time, and tiered loading keeps weights in host memory. The lesson's table takes a cold start of 328 seconds to about 15 seconds. With a 15 second start, the trial tier can scale to zero with a small loss, and the paid pool can hold one replica instead of two.

### Match the billing to the tier

The warm replicas run at high utilization, which is where per-minute billing beats per-token, above about 30 percent sustained utilization in the economics lesson. Trial bursts and the overnight batch sit below that line, so per-token or a batch tier at about half the serverless rate fits them.

### What to measure after a month

- Utilization per tier, hour by hour.
- Cold starts per day and their duration.
- Requests that missed the first-token target, and whether they fell inside a cold start.
- Trial conversions for sessions that hit a cold start against sessions that did not.
- The break-even request rate per tier from the lesson's simulator, against the measured rate.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why not give trial users the same warm pool as paid users? Expected: a warm replica costs a month of GPU hours whether trial traffic arrives or not. The decision is the conversion loss from a cold start against that cost, and the month of measurement answers it.
- **Level 4:** How does a 15 second cold start change the policy? Expected: tiers that tolerate seconds scale to zero, so the warm pool shrinks to the paths with targets of a second or two.
- **Level 4:** Which signal says a warm replica count is too low? Expected: the share of requests that miss the first-token target during scale-outs, together with the cold-start count per day.
questions.wrong:
- "Warm replicas for every tier, the cost is small." One replica per product is a month of GPU hours each. Five products idle come to thousands of hours.
- "Scale trial to zero, those users are free." A cold start of minutes on the first trial session is a lost conversion. Measure it before you decide.
- "Keep the batch pipeline warm so that it finishes earlier." Batch tolerates minutes. A warm GPU for it is paid idle time for the rest of the day.

questions.title: A lower cache threshold hits more and answers wrong
questions.prompt: Your semantic cache serves 20 percent of requests at a similarity threshold of 0.95. A teammate lowered it to 0.85 in staging. The hit rate rose to 50 percent, and a few cached answers did not fit the question asked. Which threshold do you ship, and how do you decide?
questions.short: Ship the threshold whose wrong hits you can afford, and measure that instead of guessing. A wrong cached answer is a correctness failure that a user sees, while a miss costs one model call. Keep the strict threshold on the general path, and lower it only where the answers are interchangeable or where a disclaimer is acceptable. A vendor's accuracy figure describes how often a hit was appropriate, not how often your traffic hits, so label pairs from your own traffic at both thresholds.
questions.full:
### Two numbers that get confused

The hit rate is the share of requests served from the cache. The accuracy of a hit is whether the stored answer fits the new question. The lesson warns that a vendor's accuracy claim describes match correctness, and that production hit rates are community telemetry that runs from about 10 percent on open chat to about 70 percent on structured support.

### The cost of each error

A miss costs one model call, which you know to the cent. A wrong hit costs a wrong answer in front of a user, a support ticket and some trust, and only the product can price it. The two thresholds trade one for the other.

### Decide with labeled pairs

Sample pairs of a new question and the cached answer it would receive at each threshold. Label each pair as fitting or not. At 0.85 and at 0.95 you then have a hit rate and a precision of hits. Expected saving is the hit rate times the cost of a call. Expected damage is the wrong-hit rate times the cost of a wrong answer. Ship the threshold where the second number is acceptable to the product owner.

### A two-tier scheme

The earlier caching lesson's exercise uses two thresholds: hits at 0.98 return at once, and hits at 0.90 return with a disclaimer that the answer comes from a similar earlier question. Log the tier that served each hit, and compare satisfaction per tier. This keeps the strict path strict and still takes the cheap wins.

### Why some workloads cannot go low

Code questions hit about 20 to 30 percent at best, because a small change in a code question changes the correct answer. Near-duplicate text is not near-duplicate intent there. Voice agents on a fixed prompt set reach 50 to 80 percent, because the questions really repeat.

### The checks around the threshold

Run the exact-match cache first, because a byte-identical repeat needs no embedding. Set a lifetime so that stale answers expire. The embedding cost is small, the lesson quotes a per-million-token price of 0.02 dollars for a small embedding model, so the threshold is the lever, not the embedding bill.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why is the accuracy number in a vendor's brochure not your hit rate? Expected: accuracy says how often a returned hit was appropriate. The hit rate says how often there was a hit at all, and it depends on your traffic.
- **Level 2:** What does a miss cost, and what does a wrong hit cost? Expected: a miss costs one model call. A wrong hit costs a wrong answer in front of a user, which the product has to price.
- **Level 3:** How do you lower the threshold without lowering the correctness of the strict path? Expected: a two-tier scheme, with strict matches served as they are and medium matches served with a disclaimer, and the tier logged so that satisfaction can be compared.
- **Level 3:** Why do code questions hit so rarely? Expected: a small variant in a code question changes the correct answer, so similar text is not similar intent.
questions.wrong:
- "Lower the threshold, the savings are bigger." A wrong hit is a correctness failure that a user sees. Its cost is not one model call.
- "Raise the threshold until no hit is ever wrong." The hit rate then approaches the exact-match rate, and the cache stops paying for itself.
- "Use the vendor's accuracy number as the hit rate." The figure describes match correctness, not how often your traffic hits.

questions.title: A bigger KV pool that bought nothing, until it did
questions.prompt: A teammate raised the memory fraction of a self-hosted server and grew the KV pool by 63 percent. The closed-loop benchmark at 64 concurrent users did not move. They want to revert the change, because the extra memory bought nothing. What do you tell them, and which measurement settles it?
questions.short: The benchmark never filled the pool, so the extra memory had nothing to do. At 64 users the running requests held about 11 percent of the pool, and throughput stayed within 2 percent. Under an open-loop overload the same pool mattered: at the smaller fraction the pool was 96 percent full with requests waiting outside it, and the larger pool completed about a third more requests per second. Size the pool from token usage at peak load, bursts included, and read it from the scheduler's decode lines, not from a closed-loop sweep.
questions.full:
### What the closed loop showed

The manual ran the same load sweep at a fraction of 0.7 and at 0.82 on one machine, three seeds per point. The BF16 pool grew from 234,600 to 383,065 tokens. At every concurrency the two medians were within 2 percent of each other. The decode line with the highest token usage in the whole larger-pool sweep shows why: 64 running requests held 40,751 tokens, 11 percent of the pool. On the smaller pool the highest usage in the sweep was 18 percent. A pool that is never full has nothing to give.

### What the open loop showed

The open-loop sweep offered 16 requests per second, more than the machine serves. At 0.7 the decode line read 374 running requests at a token usage of 0.96, with 101 requests waiting in the queue. At 0.82 all 480 requests of the run fit at once at a usage of 0.75, with none waiting.
